problems.title: Above the average
problems.statement_md: A cafe wants to know which drinks are priced above its average menu price. Return `item_name` and `price` for every item that costs more than the average price of all items, most expensive first, ties by `item_id`.

tables.name: menu_items
tables.description_md: One row per drink on the menu.

hints_md: You need two numbers: each item's price and the average of all prices. A query inside brackets can produce the second one.
Does an item priced exactly at the average count as 'above' it?
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** a subquery is a SELECT inside brackets that gives the outer query a value to compare with.

**Shape:** the inner query works out one number (the overall average); the outer query keeps the rows that beat it, then sorts.

**Syntax:** A bracketed `(SELECT AVG(col) FROM t)` returns a single value you can use in a comparison.

**Watch out:** an aggregate such as `AVG` cannot sit directly in a `WHERE`; and think about whether 'above' means `>` or `>=`.

solutions.label: Subquery in WHERE
solutions.explain_md: The bracketed query returns one number, the average price. `WHERE price > (...)` keeps only items above it.
solutions.sql:
SELECT item_name, price
FROM menu_items
WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM menu_items)
ORDER BY price DESC, item_id;

solutions.label: Join to a one-row table
solutions.explain_md: The subquery in FROM gives a one-row table holding the average; joining it to every item lets you compare in WHERE.
solutions.sql:
SELECT m.item_name, m.price
FROM menu_items m
CROSS JOIN (SELECT AVG(price) AS avg_price FROM menu_items) a
WHERE m.price > a.avg_price
ORDER BY m.price DESC, m.item_id;

traps.explain_md: `>=` also keeps the two items priced exactly at the average (4.50), but they are not above it.
traps.sql:
SELECT item_name, price
FROM menu_items
WHERE price >= (SELECT AVG(price) FROM menu_items)
ORDER BY price DESC, item_id;

problems.title: In a list from another table
problems.statement_md: A bookshop is planning an Irish-writers table. Return `title` and `price` of every book written by an author whose `country` is `'Ireland'`, ordered by `title`, ties by `book_id`. The country is stored in `authors`, not in `books`.

tables.name: books
tables.description_md: One row per book. `author_id` points to `authors`.

hints_md: First work out which `author_id` values belong to Irish authors. That list is the first step.
Which column of `books` should be checked against that list? Compare ids with ids.
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** a subquery can return a whole column of values, and `IN` asks 'is my value somewhere in that list?'.

**Shape:** inner query lists the matching ids from one table; the outer query keeps rows of the other table whose id is on the list.

**Syntax:** `col IN (subquery returning one column)`.

**Watch out:** match the right pair of columns; ids from different tables can overlap by accident and still run without any error.

solutions.label: IN with a subquery
solutions.explain_md: The inner query returns the ids of Irish authors. `author_id IN (...)` keeps the books whose author is on that list.
solutions.sql:
SELECT title, price
FROM books
WHERE author_id IN (SELECT author_id FROM authors WHERE country = 'Ireland')
ORDER BY title, book_id;

solutions.label: JOIN
solutions.explain_md: Joining books to authors and filtering the country gives the same rows, because each book has one author.
solutions.sql:
SELECT b.title, b.price
FROM books b
JOIN authors a ON a.author_id = b.author_id
WHERE a.country = 'Ireland'
ORDER BY b.title, b.book_id;

traps.explain_md: The list holds author ids, but `book_id` is compared with it. Book 1 and book 3 happen to have the same numbers as the Irish authors 1 and 3, so the wrong books are returned.
traps.sql:
SELECT title, price
FROM books
WHERE book_id IN (SELECT author_id FROM authors WHERE country = 'Ireland')
ORDER BY title, book_id;

problems.title: Has at least one cancellation
problems.statement_md: A clinic wants to phone patients who have cancelled at least once. Return `patient_id` and `patient_name` of every patient with one or more appointments whose `status` is `'cancelled'`. Each patient must appear once, ordered by `patient_id`.

tables.name: appointments
tables.description_md: One row per appointment. `status` is `'attended'`, `'cancelled'` or `'booked'`.

hints_md: For each patient, ask a yes/no question: is there at least one cancelled appointment that belongs to them?
A patient with two cancellations should still be one row in the answer.
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** `EXISTS` tests whether a subquery finds any row at all. It is a yes/no check, so it never multiplies rows.

**Shape:** for each patient, run a small inner query on `appointments` that links by `patient_id` and looks for the status; keep the patient if anything is found.

**Syntax:** `EXISTS (subquery)` is true when the subquery returns at least one row; link it to the outer row through a shared key.

**Watch out:** joining instead of testing existence repeats a patient once per matching row.

solutions.label: EXISTS
solutions.explain_md: For each patient the inner query looks for a cancelled appointment with the same `patient_id`. EXISTS is true or false, so a patient is never repeated.
solutions.sql:
SELECT p.patient_id, p.patient_name
FROM patients p
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM appointments a
  WHERE a.patient_id = p.patient_id AND a.status = 'cancelled'
)
ORDER BY p.patient_id;

solutions.label: IN with a subquery
solutions.explain_md: The inner query lists patient ids that have a cancellation; IN keeps each patient once however many times the id appears in the list.
solutions.sql:
SELECT patient_id, patient_name
FROM patients
WHERE patient_id IN (SELECT patient_id FROM appointments WHERE status = 'cancelled')
ORDER BY patient_id;

traps.explain_md: A plain JOIN returns one row per cancelled appointment, so Bela Horvat (two cancellations) shows up twice.
traps.sql:
SELECT p.patient_id, p.patient_name
FROM patients p
JOIN appointments a ON a.patient_id = p.patient_id
WHERE a.status = 'cancelled'
ORDER BY p.patient_id;

problems.title: Name a step with WITH
problems.statement_md: A delivery firm wants to reward couriers with big tips. Add up each courier's tips, then return `courier_name` and `total_tip` for couriers whose total is more than 20. Highest total first, ties by `courier_id`. Two different couriers can share a name.

tables.name: couriers
tables.description_md: One row per courier. Names are not unique.

tables.name: deliveries
tables.description_md: One row per delivery, with the tip left by the customer.

hints_md: Do it in two steps: first a small result with one total per courier, then use that result like a table.
Which column identifies a courier for certain: the name or the id?
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** a CTE (`WITH name AS (...)`) gives a query step a name so the next step can use it like a table.

**Shape:** step 1 = one row per courier with the total; step 2 = join that to the courier list for the names and keep the big totals.

**Syntax:** `WITH name AS (SELECT ...) SELECT ... FROM name ...` - the CTE behaves like a table for the rest of the query.

**Watch out:** group by the id, not the name. Names can repeat, and grouping by a repeated name quietly merges different people.

solutions.label: CTE
solutions.explain_md: The CTE `totals` sums tips per courier id. The main query joins it to `couriers` for the names and keeps totals above 20.
solutions.sql:
WITH totals AS (
  SELECT courier_id, SUM(tip) AS total_tip
  FROM deliveries
  GROUP BY courier_id
)
SELECT c.courier_name, t.total_tip
FROM couriers c
JOIN totals t ON t.courier_id = c.courier_id
WHERE t.total_tip > 20
ORDER BY t.total_tip DESC, c.courier_id;

solutions.label: Subquery in FROM
solutions.explain_md: The same two steps without WITH: the first step sits inside brackets in the FROM clause and gets an alias.
solutions.sql:
SELECT c.courier_name, t.total_tip
FROM couriers c
JOIN (
  SELECT courier_id, SUM(tip) AS total_tip
  FROM deliveries
  GROUP BY courier_id
) t ON t.courier_id = c.courier_id
WHERE t.total_tip > 20
ORDER BY t.total_tip DESC, c.courier_id;

traps.explain_md: Grouping by `courier_name` merges the two different couriers called Sam Ortiz (11.50 + 16.00 = 27.50), so a name appears that no single courier earned.
traps.sql:
SELECT c.courier_name, SUM(d.tip) AS total_tip
FROM couriers c
JOIN deliveries d ON d.courier_id = c.courier_id
GROUP BY c.courier_name
HAVING SUM(d.tip) > 20
ORDER BY total_tip DESC, c.courier_name;

problems.title: Top score and who holds it
problems.statement_md: A teacher wants to congratulate everyone who got the highest exam score in the class, even if several students share it. Return `student_id`, `student_name` and `score` for each student with the top score, ordered by `student_id`.

tables.name: exam_results
tables.description_md: One row per student for the term exam.

hints_md: Find the highest score on its own first. Then ask which rows have exactly that score.
Could more than one student have it?
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** `MAX` finds the top value, but it does not tell you which rows own it; a subquery lets you filter by that value.

**Shape:** inner query = the single top score; outer query = every row whose score equals it, so ties all come back.

**Syntax:** A bracketed subquery that returns one value can sit on either side of `=`.

**Watch out:** sorting and keeping the first row looks like it works, but it silently drops everyone tied for the top.

solutions.label: Subquery with MAX
solutions.explain_md: The inner query returns one number, the highest score. The outer query keeps every student whose score equals it, so both tied students appear.
solutions.sql:
SELECT student_id, student_name, score
FROM exam_results
WHERE score = (SELECT MAX(score) FROM exam_results)
ORDER BY student_id;

solutions.label: Join to the top score
solutions.explain_md: A one-row derived table holds the maximum; joining on equality keeps all students with that score.
solutions.sql:
SELECT e.student_id, e.student_name, e.score
FROM exam_results e
JOIN (SELECT MAX(score) AS top_score FROM exam_results) m ON e.score = m.top_score
ORDER BY e.student_id;

traps.explain_md: Sorting by score and taking one row returns only one of the two students who scored 94.
traps.sql:
SELECT student_id, student_name, score
FROM exam_results
ORDER BY score DESC, student_id
LIMIT 1;

problems.title: Clean up names
problems.statement_md: A shop imported customer details typed by hand, with stray spaces and mixed capitals. Return `customer_id`, `full_name` and `email`. `full_name` is the first name, one space, then the last name, all in capital letters and with no extra spaces. `email` is in lower case with no surrounding spaces. Order by `customer_id`.

tables.name: customers
tables.description_md: One row per customer, as typed in. Names and emails may have extra spaces and any capitalisation.

hints_md: Each name part may have spaces on its own edges. Clean each part before joining them.
One function removes spaces at both ends; another changes the case. Functions can be nested.
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** string functions return a cleaned-up copy of the text; the stored value is not changed.

**Shape:** tidy each name part on its own, glue the parts together with a single space, then change the case of the result.

**Syntax:** `TRIM(s)`, `UPPER(s)`, `LOWER(s)`, `CONCAT(a, ' ', b)`.

**Watch out:** trimming only after joining cannot reach spaces in the middle of the new string.

solutions.label: TRIM each part, then CONCAT
solutions.explain_md: TRIM removes spaces at both ends of each part, CONCAT joins the parts with one space, and UPPER and LOWER change the case.
solutions.sql:
SELECT customer_id,
       UPPER(CONCAT(TRIM(first_name), ' ', TRIM(last_name))) AS full_name,
       LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS email
FROM customers
ORDER BY customer_id;

solutions.label: UPPER each part, then CONCAT_WS
solutions.explain_md: CONCAT_WS puts the first argument between the others, here a single space.
solutions.sql:
SELECT customer_id,
       CONCAT_WS(' ', UPPER(TRIM(first_name)), UPPER(TRIM(last_name))) AS full_name,
       LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS email
FROM customers
ORDER BY customer_id;

traps.explain_md: Trimming the joined text only removes spaces at its two ends. A space at the end of the first name or the start of the last name stays inside, giving a double space.
traps.sql:
SELECT customer_id,
       TRIM(UPPER(CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name))) AS full_name,
       LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS email
FROM customers
ORDER BY customer_id;

problems.title: Part of a string
problems.statement_md: A book club keeps its members' email addresses. Return `member_id`, `domain` (everything after the `@`, without the `@`) and `handle_length` (how many characters come before the `@`). Order by `member_id`.

tables.name: club_members
tables.description_md: One row per member. Every `email` contains exactly one `@`.

hints_md: Find the position of the `@` first. Everything else is measured from it.
Counting characters from position 1 means the character *after* the `@` is one further along.
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** find where a marker sits in the text, then cut the text relative to that position.

**Shape:** one value gives the position of `@`; the text before it has that position minus one characters; the domain starts one character after it.

**Syntax:** `LOCATE(sub, s)`, `SUBSTRING(s, start)`, `LENGTH(s)`, `LEFT(s, n)`, `SUBSTRING_INDEX(s, delim, count)`.

**Watch out:** positions start at 1, and an off-by-one slip keeps the `@` in the domain.

solutions.label: LOCATE and SUBSTRING
solutions.explain_md: LOCATE finds the position of `@`. SUBSTRING from one position after it gives the domain, and the handle holds one fewer character than that position.
solutions.sql:
SELECT member_id,
       SUBSTRING(email, LOCATE('@', email) + 1) AS domain,
       LOCATE('@', email) - 1 AS handle_length
FROM club_members
ORDER BY member_id;

solutions.label: SUBSTRING_INDEX
solutions.explain_md: SUBSTRING_INDEX splits on a delimiter: count -1 keeps the part after the last `@`, count 1 keeps the part before the first.
solutions.sql:
SELECT member_id,
       SUBSTRING_INDEX(email, '@', -1) AS domain,
       LENGTH(SUBSTRING_INDEX(email, '@', 1)) AS handle_length
FROM club_members
ORDER BY member_id;

traps.explain_md: Starting at the `@` itself (no +1) keeps the `@` at the front of every domain.
traps.sql:
SELECT member_id,
       SUBSTRING(email, LOCATE('@', email)) AS domain,
       LOCATE('@', email) - 1 AS handle_length
FROM club_members
ORDER BY member_id;

problems.title: Rounding money
problems.statement_md: A repair shop lists invoice amounts with cents. For every invoice return `invoice_id`, `amount`, `nearest_whole` (rounded to the nearest whole number), `rounded_up` (the next whole number at or above the amount) and `rounded_down` (the whole number at or below it). Order by `invoice_id`. Refunds are stored as negative amounts.

tables.name: invoices
tables.description_md: One row per invoice. A negative `amount` is a refund.

hints_md: Three different functions answer 'nearest', 'up' and 'down'. Which is which?
Rounding down is not the same as cutting off the decimals once a number can be negative.
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** numeric functions turn a decimal into a whole number in different directions.

**Shape:** one column per direction, all computed from the same `amount`.

**Syntax:** `ROUND(x)`, `ROUND(x, 2)`, `CEIL(x)`, `FLOOR(x)`.

**Watch out:** for negative numbers, 'down' means towards minus infinity, so -2.40 goes down to -3.

solutions.label: ROUND, CEIL, FLOOR
solutions.explain_md: ROUND goes to the nearest whole number (halves go up), CEIL to the next whole number at or above, FLOOR to the next at or below.
solutions.sql:
SELECT invoice_id,
       amount,
       ROUND(amount) AS nearest_whole,
       CEIL(amount) AS rounded_up,
       FLOOR(amount) AS rounded_down
FROM invoices
ORDER BY invoice_id;

traps.explain_md: TRUNCATE just cuts off the decimals, which moves negative numbers upwards: -2.40 becomes -2 instead of -3.
traps.sql:
SELECT invoice_id,
       amount,
       ROUND(amount) AS nearest_whole,
       CEIL(amount) AS rounded_up,
       TRUNCATE(amount, 0) AS rounded_down
FROM invoices
ORDER BY invoice_id;

problems.title: Filter by year and month
problems.statement_md: A cinema wants its March 2026 sales. Return `sale_id`, `movie`, `sale_date` and `tickets` for every sale made in March 2026 (the 1st to the 31st inclusive). Order by `sale_date`, ties by `sale_id`.
hints_md: There are two ways: pull the year and month out of the date, or compare the date with a start and an end.
Which March? Check the year as well as the month.
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** a date column can be broken into parts, or compared against a range, to pick out a period.

**Shape:** keep rows from the right month of the right year; the first and last days of the month are the edge cases.

**Syntax:** `YEAR(d) = 2026`, `MONTH(d) = 3`, or `d >= 'start' AND d < 'next start'`.

**Watch out:** `MONTH(d) = 3` alone matches March of every year.

solutions.label: YEAR and MONTH
solutions.explain_md: YEAR() and MONTH() extract the parts; both must match.
solutions.sql:
SELECT sale_id, movie, sale_date, tickets
FROM ticket_sales
WHERE YEAR(sale_date) = 2026 AND MONTH(sale_date) = 3
ORDER BY sale_date, sale_id;

solutions.label: Date range
solutions.explain_md: Keeps dates from the first day of March up to, but not including, the first day of April.
solutions.sql:
SELECT sale_id, movie, sale_date, tickets
FROM ticket_sales
WHERE sale_date >= '2026-03-01' AND sale_date < '2026-04-01'
ORDER BY sale_date, sale_id;

traps.explain_md: Testing only the month number also keeps March 2025 and March 2024.
traps.sql:
SELECT sale_id, movie, sale_date, tickets
FROM ticket_sales
WHERE MONTH(sale_date) = 3
ORDER BY sale_date, sale_id;

problems.title: Days between two dates
problems.statement_md: A library wants to see how long each book was kept. Return `loan_id`, `book_title` and `days_kept`, the number of days from `borrowed_on` to `returned_on`. Order by `days_kept` from longest to shortest, ties by `loan_id`.
hints_md: There is a function that subtracts two dates and gives a number of days.
Which date goes first in the function: the earlier or the later one?
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** subtracting dates gives a count of days, which you can sort and compare like any number.

**Shape:** one extra column computed from two date columns of the same row.

**Syntax:** `DATEDIFF(later_date, earlier_date)` in MySQL (SQL Server takes `DATEDIFF(unit, earlier, later)`).

**Watch out:** swap the two dates and every answer turns negative.

solutions.label: DATEDIFF
solutions.explain_md: DATEDIFF(a, b) is a minus b in days, so the return date goes first.

traps.explain_md: With the arguments the wrong way round, every result is negative, so the sort order flips too.

problems.title: Replace missing values
problems.statement_md: A garden centre prepares a pay and badge list. Return `staff_id`, `display_name` and `total_pay`. `display_name` is the `nickname` if there is one, otherwise the `staff_name`. `total_pay` is `salary` plus `bonus`, where a missing bonus counts as 0. Order by `staff_id`.

tables.name: staff
tables.description_md: One row per employee. `nickname` and `bonus` are NULL when there is none.

hints_md: Some nickname and bonus values are NULL. A function can swap a NULL for a fallback value.
What is `2300 + NULL`?
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** NULL means 'unknown', and any arithmetic with NULL gives NULL. A fallback value fixes that for display or sums.

**Shape:** two computed columns, each replacing NULL with a sensible default.

**Syntax:** `COALESCE(a, b, ...)` returns the first non-NULL; `IFNULL(a, b)` is the two-argument MySQL form.

**Watch out:** a 0 bonus is a real value and is not NULL.

solutions.label: COALESCE
solutions.explain_md: COALESCE returns the first value that is not NULL: the nickname or else the name, and the bonus or else 0.
solutions.sql:
SELECT staff_id,
       COALESCE(nickname, staff_name) AS display_name,
       salary + COALESCE(bonus, 0) AS total_pay
FROM staff
ORDER BY staff_id;

solutions.label: IFNULL and CASE
solutions.explain_md: IFNULL is MySQL's two-argument version. A CASE expression says the same thing step by step.
solutions.sql:
SELECT staff_id,
       IFNULL(nickname, staff_name) AS display_name,
       CASE WHEN bonus IS NULL THEN salary ELSE salary + bonus END AS total_pay
FROM staff
ORDER BY staff_id;

traps.explain_md: `salary + bonus` is NULL whenever the bonus is NULL, so those employees show no pay at all.
traps.sql:
SELECT staff_id,
       COALESCE(nickname, staff_name) AS display_name,
       salary + bonus AS total_pay
FROM staff
ORDER BY staff_id;

problems.title: Combine two lists
problems.statement_md: A bookshop wants one mailing list from two sources: its newsletter and its workshop sign-ups. Return a single column `email` with every address that is in either list, each address once, in alphabetical order.
hints_md: You are stacking one result on top of another, not matching rows side by side.
Stacking has two flavours. One keeps repeats; the other removes them.
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** set operators stack the rows of two queries that have the same number of columns.

**Shape:** `SELECT` the column from each table, stack them, and sort the final result once at the end.

**Syntax:** `query1 UNION query2` removes duplicates; `query1 UNION ALL query2` keeps every row.

**Watch out:** the one `ORDER BY` goes after the last query and sorts the combined result.

solutions.label: UNION
solutions.explain_md: UNION stacks the two lists and removes duplicate rows, so each address appears once.
solutions.sql:
SELECT email FROM newsletter
UNION
SELECT email FROM workshop_signups
ORDER BY email;

solutions.label: UNION ALL then DISTINCT
solutions.explain_md: UNION ALL keeps every row; wrapping it in a query with DISTINCT removes the repeats afterwards.
solutions.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT email
FROM (
  SELECT email FROM newsletter
  UNION ALL
  SELECT email FROM workshop_signups
) all_emails
ORDER BY email;

traps.explain_md: UNION ALL keeps every row, so addresses in both lists (and repeated sign-ups) are listed more than once.
traps.sql:
SELECT email FROM newsletter
UNION ALL
SELECT email FROM workshop_signups
ORDER BY email;
